column6: This is an important issue, and needs addressing, but it is luckily tempered by an 'ambivalent' middle. It is mostly the 10% of extremists on each end of a spectrum that are most problematic, so hopefully solvable. But this issue helps to drive the issue of Populism and Nationalistic Leaders. The two are deeply intertwined, and given the disproportionate power of leaders vs people, the leaders issue is more severe, yet cannot be uncoupled from the social divisions issue. Need more incentives that drive social common ground rather than division and outrage.
column11: Important issue, well documented, and ties in with other issues of 'truth' and 'social division' etc. Solutions needed, as although not obviously a civilisational risk, these issues all seem on the face of it to be risk amplifiers across many risks, and seem to be influencing leadership's beliefs or at least stated beliefs, hence the high rating.

column111: This issue is connected in complex ways to both the 'social division' issue and the 'populist nationalistic leaders' issue. Although some are skeptical of the importance: https://80000hours.org/podcast/episodes/hugo-mercier-misinformation-mass-persuasion/ my intuition is that this is particularly salient for global catastrophe. This is because 'truth-tracking' (ie an appropriate correspondence between one's/society's beliefs and the way the world is in fact) is important for adaptation and survival. The more that belief diverges from 'truth' the more vulnerable a society becomes. Note that the beliefs don't have to be literally true, but beliefs need to have an appropriate adaptive action-driving correspondence to the way the world is (note that useful myths etc aren't necessarily true, but lead to adaptive behaviour).

column271: Overreliance on certain systems without backup plan is rife. Communications critical to managing many catastrophes, including de-escalating conflict. Plausible ways comms could fail, including electromagnetic pulse etc. World needs a Plan B in the internet age.
column276: Major obstacle to mitigating many catastrophes. Game theoretically challenging. Solutions potentially exist (eg distributed digital tools, coordination optimising approaches) but deeply tied to the 'entrenchment of elites' issue and 'populism and nationalism' issue. Unlikely to properly solve many GCR risks without overcoming this in some way or other. Whether by strengthening or abandoning current global governance systems and trying something radically new. Individual and national incentives all pull the world away from such a solution though. See the 'Moloch' problem.
column281: Important issue that doesn't depend on AI but will be amplified by AI. Though some are very skeptical, eg: Hugo Mercier.
column286: Well known issue. And a side-effect of other more proximal issues that are probably more relevant to address. Need to be prepared to adapt over decades to century time scale. Humans have achieved this before in many locations.
column291: I think there is a lot of wilful denial, but adaptations will occur driven by economic incentives, a shift to more appropriate cropping for regional conditions etc. A shift from less calorie dense animal agriculture to more calorie dense cropping. Major farming shifts can be quick and follow incentives, eg 'dairy conversion' in New Zealand over a period of 1 to 2 decades. Other transitions are possible.
column296: Not an expert on this issue, but my intuition is that impacts would be localised and reveal themselves in time to act.
column301: Governments are not often in the business of seeing the dynamics of government functioning as a key risk. There definitely seems to be a trend to increasing risk and decreasing capability to deal with risk, especially at a cooperative international level. Prisoners dilemma etc.

This trend interacts with other critical trends such as nuclear weapons, nationalistic leaders, social divisions, radicalisation, reduced state capability etc.
column316: Interacts with the 'entrenchment of global elite' item. Could lead to hard economic landing and suffering, from which a more constrained economy/society is likely to emerge from.
column321: Well known issue. Would benefit from state investment. But human populations thrived in the pre-antibiotic era, so this is not a civilisation level threat.
column326: Yes, though the risks remain theoretical, unlike the risks of AWS without oversight, which is already taking off.

column361: Automation has been proceeding for decades, not aware of any actual loss of critical knowledge in a civilisation threatening way.
column366: Widely recognised as one of the biggest issues in the world today. Particularly concerning as potentially 'unhinged' leaders with nationalistic goals could easily precipitate a range of other catastrophes. The leaders feed on populism (and this causes more wild policy claims) and the populism feeds on the 'cult' psychology of the leaders (in group, out group, all kinds of dynamics). This is a feed-forward, and contagious, loop and something needs to break it.
column371: Such events will almost certainly happen, but like Fukushima, will have limited localised impacts (when compared with global catastrophe), or the world will quickly adapt to workarounds. There's not really a mechanism for 'scale-up' of impacts from local natural hazards to become global civilisational risks.

column386: Global food system security is needed, this is the crux of many potential GCRs. Wide-ranging benefits from addressing it.
column391: Great power tensions are all trending in the wrong direction, there is high risk of escalation, but many many diplomats are already working on these issues.
column396: Well known issue, many resources spent on negotiating treaties etc. However, risk remains, and interacts with other risks that drive escalation of conflicts.
column401: Nuclear war could have diverse impacts and nuclear famine is one possible outcome. I think the trend towards the risk of nuclear war rising is more important to deal with, and impacts on communication systems, trade systems, geopolitics, etc are all important, nuclear famine is one theoretical risk, though very serious and the world has no Plan for it. Also relevant to 'food shocks' more generally and improving global food security.
column406: Much more should be done to assess this given the potential dire consequences, however, it is not clear that AI is in fact being embedded in such systems. Need more concerted effort at global level to curb influence of nationalism beyond its own borders. Also need more effort to dampen the drivers of populist nationalism, perhaps something to do with platform media, unclear cause or solutions.
column416: This is important and goes hand in hand with the 'Populist and Nationalistic Leaders' item. There is still no good global mechanism to enforce global norms. Consequently many measures directed at GCRs, eg the Paris Climate Accord, end up toothless, and ineffective. Not to mention norms like the Geneva Convention, which are routinely violated, leading to escalation of conflict.
column421: I understand the concern, but the pathway to global catastrophe isn't so clear. Probably education systems will adapt, and it's not obvious that democracy is necessary to avoid suffering and catastrophe.
column426: Climate adaptation is one of the biggest topics in the world. I think social division and inequality are incredibly important issues and may well foster the conditions that create greater risk for a greater number of people. That said, I think this scenario overdetermines the root of the issue as being one of polarization - which probably ascribes cause to something that is in large part a symptom - and suggests that we are experiencing a unique ahistorical degradation from a good united society to a fractured one. I'd draw attention to critical analyses of both populism and technocracy that emphasize how consensus without parity requires surrender of one or another party. 
It's also facile to point towards Russia as being a state particularly guilty of manipulating information in a harmful way. Yes, Russia is clearly an authoritarian and largely horrible state - but it is by no means alone in its wielding of information for political objectives.

the contest over what counts as real information in these submissions is genuinely fascinating. 
i think there needs to be focused attention on ensuring that really quite different issues aren't bundled together. doing so smuggles in a whole heap of preferences, political commitments and normative preferences without acknowledging their prominence. 
deepfakes seem plausibly to have a deleterious effect. polarization of politics, opinion and media coverage could take a variety of forms and not all of them imply a worsening of our risk landscape, given the clear case that can be made for status quo politics resulting in crises and degredation. 
trust - whether between people in a society, a society and its govt and media, or between states cannot be predicated on an aspiration for an uncontestable truth - it needs to be predicated on the fostering of trust in a far more meaningful process of interaction. 
i'm not taking a post-truth or post-modern stance here, by the way. i'm instead stating that, as much as we might wish to, it is not necessarily possible or desirable to draw a line around some issues as "technical" when the issues at hand rely on political action to address them.
